Iran: the IAEA no longer knows where an underground uranium enrichment plant is, and an LNG tanker hits a mine in Hormuz

On Friday, November 13, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it was “increasingly concerned” about an underground enrichment plant in Isfahan that it has never been able to inspect. The same day, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed that an LNG tanker had hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz [1][2][5].

In its latest report, sent to member states on Friday, the IAEA, the UN nuclear watchdog, writes that it knows neither the exact location of the Isfahan plant, declared by Iran last year, nor whether it contains nuclear material [1][2][3]. The report does not establish that uranium is being enriched there [2].

Before the US and Israeli strikes of June 2025, the agency estimated that Iran held 440.9 kilos of uranium enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade; no one knows what has become of this stockpile [1][2]. The agency has “lost continuity of knowledge” about these reserves for more than a year, writes its director, Rafael Grossi [1].

Tehran replies that inspections cannot resume in the face of “persistent, explicit and public threats” from the US president [4]. National security chief Mohsen Rezaei vows that not “a single particle” of enriched uranium will leave the country [3].

In the strait, the Revolutionary Guards navy claims that an LNG tanker, carrying liquefied natural gas, ignored its warnings, took the southern route and “exploded very violently” on a mine [5]. Neither the ship's name nor the explosion has been independently confirmed [5].
According to the Washington Institute, cited by Reuters, at least 10 ships were hit in the strait from November 1 to 10 [5].

Donald Trump says he could destroy Iran's energy, bridges and factories in three days, but is holding back his strikes at the request of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Bahrain: “I could end it immediately, but at the request of the countries I want to protect, we are taking a slightly longer path” [6].

Oil is falling nonetheless: on Friday morning, Brent was trading around $95 to $96 a barrel, heading for a second weekly decline, weighed down by rising US inventories and a larger global surplus forecast by the International Energy Agency [7].

Key takeaway: the guns have partly fallen silent, but Iran keeps two levers that Washington does not control: a missing stockpile of highly enriched uranium, and the ability to make Hormuz dangerous for ships [2][5].

Without inspectors, there is no way to check whether Iran is rebuilding a program capable of leading to a bomb; the IAEA says it is ready to return “at short notice” [1]. Trump, for his part, says he no longer needs a deal and has removed Vice President J.D. Vance from the talks [10].

Diplomacy remains stalled: Mohsen Rezaei is waiting for a US response to seven conditions and repeats that Hormuz will not reopen before then [8]. Qatar and Pakistan are continuing their mediation [9].

What does it mean for me? Despite the mines, oil prices are falling, because the market is betting that the worst is over and sees too much oil in the world [7]. Yet one explosion too many on an oil tanker or LNG carrier could quickly push fuel and gas prices back up, and with them your energy bill.

In Dublin, the EU entrusts peace in Ukraine to five countries and Brussels, but is still stuck on the €45 billion needed for Kyiv

On Friday, November 13 in Dublin, the 27 decided that Europe would be represented at future negotiations on Ukraine by the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the EU institutions. However, Kyiv's funding for 2027 remains blocked by Friedrich Merz's ultimatum and the refusal of four countries [1][4][5].

The European team will bring together the so-called “E5” group, five major military powers including the United Kingdom, which is not an EU member, plus the Commission and the European Council, announced António Costa, President of the European Council [1][4]. The representatives would probably be the national security advisers of the five countries [1].

“Europe must speak with one voice, clear and united,” said António Costa, recalling that only Ukraine can decide on its territory and sovereignty [4]. Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission, welcomed a “Team Europe: E5 plus EU institutions” [4].

This formula rules out the idea of a single envoy [3]. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas had put herself forward; sending her was “simply impossible,” according to a senior diplomat cited by Reuters [1]. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had revived the debate, arguing that the proliferation of formats was hurting Europe's credibility [1].

On money, Ukraine needs about €70 billion more in 2027, and the EU will have to find roughly €45 billion of it [7]. The 2028-2034 EU budget, which was not officially on the agenda, was discussed at length [5].

Friedrich Merz is sticking to his idea: tying Germany's contribution to the EU budget to a commitment by all states to fund Ukraine. He says he received broad support, but Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin expressed reservations [5]. Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria made it clear from the outset that they did not want to pay, according to Agence Europe [5].

The leaders also discussed artificial intelligence: Ursula von der Leyen announced seven AI “gigafactories,” huge computing centers [7]. Spain's Pedro Sánchez, campaigning for the November 29 general election, did not attend [2].

Key takeaway: Europe, kept out of the Abu Dhabi talks between Americans, Russians and Ukrainians, is finally organizing itself to get a seat at the table, relying on its big armies rather than a single negotiator [1][3].

The choice remains fragile: the Kremlin says it will only accept an expanded format once convinced of the Europeans' willingness to contribute to peace [1]. And Russia wants to discuss the entire European security architecture, which Kaja Kallas sees as a maneuver to divert attention from a ceasefire [1].

The budget issue is even weightier: without a deal, Ukraine faces a funding gap in 2027, and the German ultimatum threatens the negotiation of the seven-year EU budget [5][7]. The 27 are due to decide at the European Council on November 26 and 27 [7].

France is one of the five countries that will speak on Europe's behalf: its voice will carry weight in the terms of any peace. As for your wallet, the €45 billion needed for Kyiv will come from the EU budget or from joint borrowing, guaranteed by taxpayers in the member states, including you.

China: in Bangkok, Li Qiang signs eight agreements with Thailand, from durian to electric cars, before facing ASEAN in Manila

Chinese Premier Li Qiang began on Friday, November 13 in Bangkok the first official visit to Thailand by a Chinese head of government in seven years. Eight agreements were signed with Anutin Charnvirakul, covering fruit, cars, security and training. On Sunday, Li heads to Manila for the China-ASEAN summit [1][4].
Li Qiang is on an official visit from November 13 to 15, a first for a Chinese premier in seven years [1][4].

On Friday, at Government House in Bangkok, Li and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul witnessed the signing of eight cooperation documents [1][5]. Bangkok had approved seven of them before the visit [6].

The most anticipated concerns durian, the star of Thai exports: a new protocol replaces the 2004 agreement and extends pest controls from orchards to packing houses [1]. Salak (“snake fruit”) gets its very first protocol, a market worth at least 76 million baht a year according to Bangkok [6].

Four texts cover standards and weights and measures for agricultural products, sanitary checks on durian and salak, and food safety [5]. The others concern electric and connected vehicles, vocational training, security and lifting the cap of 12 staff per consulate general [1][6].

Li Qiang said he was ready to “consolidate mutual political trust” [3]. He wants to make progress on the Belt and Road Initiative, cooperate in finance, new energy, semiconductors and AI, and speed up negotiations on a new five-year economic and trade plan [2].

Rail links between China, Laos and Thailand, with possible extensions to Malaysia and Singapore, featured prominently in the talks [1]. In July, the two countries pledged to speed up the first phase of the Thailand-China high-speed rail line and to launch the second [1].
China is Thailand's largest trading partner: $153.26 billion in trade in 2025, up 14.4% year on year, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry [4].

Key takeaway: on the eve of the ASEAN summit, Beijing is courting a friendly Southeast Asian country and leaves with concrete agreements, at a time when its relations with the Philippines, the summit's host, remain tense in the South China Sea [7][8].

For Thailand, the stakes are primarily agricultural. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow presented China as a key partner and export market, highlighting investment in AI and electric cars and the opening of the Chinese market to Thai fruit [10].

For China, it is a showcase: Li arrives in Manila on Sunday for the 29th China-ASEAN summit, on November 15 and 16, with AI and energy security on the agenda according to spokesperson Guo Jiakun [4][7][8]. In October, Beijing had accused Manila of “setting up multiple obstacles” to its participation in an ASEAN meeting, which the Philippine defense secretary had rejected [8].

For you, the direct effect is small. But Thailand is a car manufacturing hub where Chinese electric car makers are setting up: their low-cost models gain a springboard there to global markets, competing with European brands.

Gulf: Qatar places itself under Turkey's wing with a mutual defense pact signed in Istanbul

On Friday, November 13 in Istanbul, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, signed a mutual defense agreement: the two countries pledge a common position in the face of any external armed attack against either of them, in the midst of the war between the United States and Iran [1][2][3].

The signing took place at Dolmabahçe Palace, during the 12th meeting of the Supreme Strategic Committee between the two countries; the emir had come from COP31, the UN climate conference held in Antalya [4][8].

According to the Turkish presidency, cited by Reuters, Ankara and Doha commit to consulting each other on threats to their security, on regional and global security issues and on their defense policies [2].

The pact also provides for more joint military exercises, stronger cooperation between their defense industries and personnel training [2]. Its full text has not been published; it is one of five agreements signed the same day [2][4].
The two countries also want to expand their energy trade, particularly in liquefied natural gas [5].

Erdogan said the two countries would keep working to prevent a new war in the Gulf and for dialogue; Doha speaks of a “strategic partnership” [8]. The Qatari Foreign Ministry also condemned Israeli violations in Gaza [6].

Turkey already has troops in Qatar, and six Turkish F-16 fighter jets have been stationed at Dukhan Air Base since July 2024, according to the Pakistani daily Dawn [7]. A Turkish analyst cited by Al Jazeera expects deliveries of Turkish weapons and air defenses to Qatar in the short term [1].

This pact adds to a series of alliances: in August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a mutual assistance pact, and in October, Qatar, Indonesia, Pakistan and Turkey signed a defense memorandum in Doha [5][8].
Key takeaway: a wealthy Gulf emirate, a mediator between Washington and Tehran, is seeking an extra security guarantee from Turkey, a NATO member, in a region where attacks are multiplying [1][5].

Qatar was targeted in 2025 by Israeli and Iranian attacks, which exposed the limits of its Washington-based security strategy [10]. With the war against Iran, Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and attacks on tankers in the Gulf, the monarchies are piling up insurance policies [1][5].

For Turkey, it is a gain in influence in the Gulf and an outlet for its defense industries, which the pact plans to bring closer to Qatar's [2][7]. One unknown remains: what the Turkish commitment would actually be worth against Israel or Iran, since the text has not been made public [4].

What does it mean for me? Qatar exports liquefied gas and acts as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran. Anything that reduces the risk of an escalation affecting its facilities also limits the risk of an energy price spike in Europe. For the European defense industry, however, it means a Turkish competitor gaining ground in the Gulf.

ASEAN: Trump, Li Qiang, Takaichi, Lula and Carney expected in Manila, where Southeast Asia wants to sign the first major regional digital agreement

The 49th summit of ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, opens on Sunday, November 15 in Manila. Donald Trump, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Japan's Sanae Takaichi, Brazil's Lula and Canada's Mark Carney are expected. The Philippines hopes to conclude a binding regional agreement on the digital economy [1][4][5].

The summit and its side meetings are being held at the Philippine International Convention Center in Metro Manila. Dates vary by source: from November 15 to 17 according to the Malaysian ambassador, and through the 18th including side meetings according to others [1][3][4][5].
The Philippines chairs ASEAN in 2026 under the slogan “Navigating Our Future, Together” [1].
Expected outcome: the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), presented as the world's first binding region-wide agreement on the digital economy [1].

Donald Trump, Lula and Mark Carney are among the confirmed leaders, as is UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres [1][4]. Xi Jinping will not attend: Li Qiang is leading the Chinese delegation at the 29th China-ASEAN summit on November 15 and 16 [4][8].

Sanae Takaichi is attending a Japan-ASEAN summit before heading to APEC in Shenzhen [7]. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is leading his country's delegation, but will return early to host Emmanuel Macron on November 17 [5].
According to Thai public broadcaster Thai PBS, the leaders are preparing a joint response to the crisis in the Middle East [6].
Preparations were 90-95% complete according to the organizers, and Executive Secretary Ralph Recto inspected the venues in Pasay [1][3].

Key takeaway: for three days, Manila becomes the crossroads of the great powers, just before the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Washington, Beijing and Tokyo are testing their alliances in Southeast Asia there [4][7].

The atmosphere is tense between the Philippines and China: in October, Beijing had accused Manila of “setting up multiple obstacles” to its participation in an ASEAN meeting, which the Philippine defense secretary had rejected [8]. Li Qiang is coming nonetheless, with AI and energy security on the agenda, according to Chinese spokesperson Guo Jiakun [8].

A “binding” agreement requires signatory countries to apply the same rules, in this case for the digital economy: that is what sets it apart from ASEAN's usual mere declarations of intent [1]. For businesses, it promises a common framework across the region, instead of disparate national rules.
The Philippines is also staking its image: the summit is meant to showcase its leadership role and its ability to attract new investment [1].

For you, ASEAN is a fast-growing workshop of the world: clothing, electronics, auto parts. A regional digital agreement would make online sales and the establishment of European companies in the region easier, and the major decisions Trump and Li Qiang make there can affect the prices of many imported products.

The US 2-year yield is having its biggest week in more than two years: the Fed could raise rates by half a point in December

The yield on 2-year US Treasury bonds, the most sensitive to Federal Reserve (Fed) decisions, posted its biggest rise in more than two years this week, reaching 4.892%. The causes: stubborn inflation and Fed Governor Christopher Waller, who does not rule out a half-point hike [3][4].

On Tuesday, November 10, after hotter-than-expected inflation, US yields posted their biggest rise in 19 months, according to CNN [1]. The 2-year yield jumped 17 basis points (0.17 point), from 4.56% to 4.73% [2].

Over two sessions, the 2-year yield gained 34 basis points, its biggest two-day rise in three and a half years [4]. On Friday, it was heading for its biggest weekly rise in more than two years, after peaking at 4.892%, its highest since October 14 [3].

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he did not rule out a half-point (50 basis point) hike in December [4]. According to World Today Journal, he could back it if core inflation stays at 0.3% a month or more; Stephen Stanley of Santander still expects a quarter point [5].
Markets were pricing a 14.5% chance of a large hike next month, compared with 0% the previous week [4].
On Friday, October producer prices rose 0.3% month on month, slightly less than the expected 0.4%, but 6.5% year on year, the highest since November 2022 [6].
The 10-year yield, the benchmark for US mortgages, climbed back above 5% on Thursday, to 5.125%, and approached 5.16% on Friday [7][12].
Key takeaway: markets are no longer asking whether the Fed will raise rates in December, but by how much. The 2-year yield, which closely tracks these decisions, is the best gauge [3][4].
A rise in the policy rate makes money more expensive for everyone: mortgages, business loans, credit cards. It slows activity to bring inflation down, but also weighs on the stock market [7][12].
The move crosses the Atlantic: when US bonds pay more, investors also demand more to lend to European governments, including France, and the dollar strengthens against the euro [4][7].
The next key date is the Fed meeting on December 8 and 9, where markets see a hike as a done deal [7].

For you, rising US rates eventually affect your borrowing: European rates partly follow, which makes fixed-rate mortgages more expensive. Conversely, savings accounts and euro-denominated life insurance funds can pay more when rates rise. A stronger dollar also makes gasoline more expensive. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: the 2-year yield, the Fed's thermometer

When you buy a 2-year government bond, you lend to the government for two years. Its yield depends mainly on what investors expect from the Fed's policy rate over that period: if a hike is looming, they demand more, and the yield rises [3]. Since the price of an already-issued bond moves in the opposite direction to its yield, a sharp rise in rates makes bonds already held lose value [3][4]. The 10-year yield depends more on long-term inflation and growth; it is the one that guides mortgages [7]. When the 2-year jumps 34 basis points in two days, it is a sign that the market has abruptly changed its mind about the Fed [4].
Precedents: when rates soar
The Fed raises rates at a forced pace to fight inflation; the Nasdaq loses 33.1% over the year, its worst year since 2008, and the S&P 500 nearly 20% [10].
A series of rapid rate hikes can drag growth stocks down for an entire year [10].

The 10-year US Treasury yield briefly crosses 5% for the first time since July 2007; Wall Street falls [8].
At the end of October 2023, the S&P 500 closes about 10% below its July record, a “correction” triggered by high yields [9].

US employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs: stocks jump, as investors hope the Fed will not have to raise rates [11].
Three months later, the scenario has reversed: stubborn inflation, bets on a hike and a soaring 2-year yield [3][6].

The government officially confirmed its intention to remove the measure that had caused particular discontent in the education sector, following a long meeting with the unions [1].

news.2026-11-14-perou-banque-centrale-ha: Peru: the central bank raises its rate for the first time in 45 months, with inflation at a three-year high

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru raised its policy rate from 4.25% to 4.50%, after 14 months without change. Inflation climbed to 5.3% year on year in October, driven by food, energy and El Niño [1][2][3].
Announced on November 12, the quarter-point hike is the first in 45 months and ends 14 months of holding steady [4][5].
Annual inflation rose from 4.5% in September to 5.3% in October, its highest level in three years, mainly due to food and energy prices [2][5].
The bank's board cites supply shocks, rising inflation expectations and buoyant domestic demand [1], without promising further hikes [3].
BBVA Research also cites the lingering effects of El Niño and tensions in the Middle East, and does not rule out a further adjustment [6].
Key takeaway: by raising its rate, the central bank makes credit more expensive to curb demand and prevent the surge in food prices from becoming embedded in expectations [1].

The shock comes largely from outside, from the climate with El Niño and from energy with tensions in the Middle East, over which a central bank has little control [6]: the hike is mainly aimed at preventing contagion to other prices [1].
Little direct effect for you. But the Peruvian case shows how a climate event and a distant war can end up pushing up a country's interest rates.
